protocol_and_eligibility.research_question: What does this review assess: the benefits and harms of patient-specific cutting guides versus conventional cutting guides or computer-assisted surgical navigation in people undergoing primary TKA?
protocol_and_eligibility.eligibility_inclusion_criteria: Types of studies We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs). We included studies reported as full text, those published as abstracts only, and unpublished data. There was no language restriction. Types of participants We included adults undergoing primary TKA for advanced arthritis due to any cause, including osteoarthritis, post-traumatic arthritis, or inflammatory arthritis. We excluded participants receiving TKA for tumours, unicompartmental replacement or revision knee replacement. We excluded participants undergoing TKA following either a previous osteotomy or previous unicompartmental replacement arthroplasty on the same knee. Types of interventions We included RCTs comparing total knee arthroplasty performed using patient-specific guides versus conventional instrumentation or computer-assisted surgery. The technique, patient-specific cutting guides (PSGs), is a technology used in TKA whereby preoperative imaging (magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), computerised tomography (CT) scans and plain radiographs) is used to create anatomic three- dimensional models of the patient's knee (Ast 2012). PSGs are then manufactured based on these personalised models. These models are fitted to the bone surfaces during surgery to permit the facilitation of bone resections based on preoperatively planned resection angles of the femur and tibia. Using PSG to perform TKA differs from both NAV and CON. There is no requirement to place reference pins in the shaft of the femur and tibia as seen in NAV, whilst it negates the need to instrument the intramedullary canal of femur or tibia as seen in CON. protocol_and_eligibility.eligibility_exclusion_criteria: We excluded participants receiving TKA for tumours, unicompartmental replacement or revision knee replacement. It was not possible to blind any of the persons involved in the study to group allocation due to the required preoperative CT scan. It was not possible to blind the surgeon due to the nature of the surgical instrumentation.
